analysis.one_liner: Directs the FCC to cap price-gouging phone rates charged to families of prison inmates.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced by Rep. Bobby Rush with no cosponsors in the final month of the 112th Congress, never got a hearing or a vote and died in committee.
analysis.plain_summary: Phone calls from prison are among the most expensive calls in America, sometimes $1 a minute plus $3 to connect, and the families who receive them are usually low-income. A single phone company typically holds the exclusive contract at each prison, and it shares revenue with the facility as a commission, which pushes prices up. The bill would have required the Federal Communications Commission to set rules capping rates, banning those commissions, requiring collect and prepaid calling options, and letting more than one company serve each facility.
analysis.who_benefits: Families of incarcerated people, who are typically low-income and pay the cost of collect calls and prepaid accounts. The bill's own findings note that staying in touch reduces recidivism, so inmates themselves, their communities, and the broader public also stand to gain.

how_it_helps.text: Directs the FCC to consider caps on per-minute and per-call charges for interstate calls from prisons, where rates reach $1 per minute plus $3 connection fees.

Would ban commissions that inmate phone providers pay to correctional facilities for exclusive rights, commissions that in some cases reach 60 percent of revenue and are effectively passed on to calling families.
Would require providers to offer both collect calling and debit (prepaid) accounts, and to let more than one carrier serve each facility so prisoners have a choice.
The bill's findings state that frequent family contact reduces recidivism and that excessive rates burden and sometimes prevent that contact.

analysis.who_pays: Inmate telephone companies and correctional agencies that collect the commissions would give up revenue. Any rate cap shrinks what the exclusive carrier can charge. The cost to the public is indirect: if facility budgets leaned on those commissions, states or localities might have to replace them.
analysis.who_pays_short: Prison phone companies and prison commissions

drawbacks.text: The bill does not itself set rates; it only requires the FCC to 'consider' specified forms of regulation, so relief would depend entirely on what the Commission adopted within one year.
Banning commissions would cut revenue that correctional agencies currently receive, which those agencies and some prison officials argued funds programs and costs of monitoring inmate calls.
The bill would preempt state rules on interstate inmate phone commissions, taking away rules some states had already adopted.
With zero cosponsors and introduction in the last month of a two-year Congress, the bill had no realistic path even if it had moved.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is concrete and immediate: lower phone bills for low-income families keeping ties with imprisoned relatives. The main cost is a transfer of revenue away from prison phone contractors and correctional agencies, which is exactly the mechanism inflating the rates in the first place. The design is weak — 'consider' rather than 'set' — but it was aimed at a documented price-gouging structure.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Energy and Commerce Committee and its Communications subcommittee on the day it was introduced, and no hearing, markup, or floor vote ever happened before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Bobby Rush introduced the bill on November 30, 2012, in the final month of the 112th Congress.
It was referred that day to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce and to its Subcommittee on Communications and Technology, and never advanced further.
The bill's findings cite per-minute charges reaching $1 and $3 connection charges, and commissions to prison administrators of up to 60 percent of payphone revenue, as the drivers of excessive rates.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The inmate telephone companies and the correctional agencies that collect commission revenue kept their exclusive contracts and their pricing structure, since no committee action or vote ever occurred.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Prison phone companies and commission-collecting agencies

for.name: Rep. Bobby L. Rush
for.role: Sponsor, House Energy and Commerce Committee member
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to his own committee, with no cosponsors signing on.

against.name: Rep. Fred Upton
against.role: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill, which sat in committee until the Congress ended on January 3, 2013.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was introduced by one Democrat in a chamber where the committee agenda was controlled by Republicans; with zero cosponsors, no record vote or party split ever occurred.

industries.note: Companies holding exclusive contracts at prisons charged some of the highest call rates in the country; the bill threatened rate caps, a commission ban, and competition at each facility. Their business model depends on the very structure the bill targeted.

State and local corrections departments receive commission payments of up to 60 percent of inmate phone revenue for granting exclusive rights; the bill would have banned those payments and preempted conflicting state rules.
